items.title: How much does waiting to send a confirmation change how it reads?
items.description: Drag how many days pass between the verbal decision and the written confirmation being sent. Per L2, the closer a confirmation is sent to the original conversation, the more it reads as routine practice rather than a reaction to trouble — a message sent the same day (Version B in L3) reads as professional; one sent only after a problem has already surfaced (Version A, effectively never sent until the incident review, three weeks later) reads as defensive.

params.name: daysDelayed
params.label: Days between the decision and the confirmation

items.compute: const routinePerception = Math.max(10, 100 - params.daysDelayed * 5); return { routinePerception };

outputs.label: Reads as routine practice, not reactive

items.title: Does this decision actually need a written confirmation?
items.description: Per L2's flowchart, a verbal decision only calls for a written confirmation when stakes and ambiguity are both high — either one alone isn't enough. Drag how much goes wrong if this decision is later misremembered or disputed (stakes), and how hard it would be to remember exactly without help (ambiguity). The need score only climbs when both are high together, same as the Scenario's 'skip the security review' decision (high stakes, easy to misremember a hallway chat) versus the Checkpoint's variable-rename example (near-zero stakes, zero ambiguity thanks to the diff).

params.name: stakes
params.label: Stakes if this is misremembered or disputed later

params.name: ambiguity
params.label: How hard this would be to remember exactly, unaided

outputs.label: How strongly this calls for a written confirmation
